To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the probability that a given word will be used as a continuation of a sentence fragment can be estimated from event-related brain activity recorded during reading of that sentence fragment.
the brain can pre-activate the meaning of individual words during language comprehension and that the strength of this pre-activation can be predicted by offline probabilities of word occurrence.
readers' brains pre-activate words that are more likely than others to follow the sentence fragment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the human brain processes the meaning of written language.
the role of probabilistic word pre-activations in language comprehension and how these pre-activations can be measured using brain potentials.
the cognitive processes underlying human language comprehension and the role of anticipation in these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain is capable of anticipating words during language processing.
the brain is capable of anticipating words during language comprehension.
the brain is a probabilistic machine that is constantly anticipating the future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
readers' brains pre-activate words in a graded manner that is proportional to their likelihood of being given as a continuation of a sentence fragment.
we show how the brain can use the information available to it to anticipate upcoming events.
the brain anticipates the upcoming word in the sentence, and this anticipation is graded by the probability of the words.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a simple passive receiver of sensory input.
readers' brains do indeed anticipate upcoming words during language comprehension, and that the degree to which they do so can be quantified.

language processing is not a passive bottom-up process, but rather a dynamic interplay between top-down and bottom-up processing, in which readers use their knowledge of the world and their expectations to predict the upcoming words.
